title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L II.1, Theodicy, SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Babylonian Theodicy, dialogue: 258 of 288 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (10 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
The sufferer complains that he is an orphan, poor and oppressed while the wicked prosper; his friend answers that the ways of the gods are unknowable and that the pious are rewarded in the end. At the close the friend concedes that the gods made humans prone to falsehood, and the sufferer asks for mercy from his god and goddess.

The Babylonian Theodicy is a dialogue in 27 stanzas of 11 lines between a sufferer and his friend about the injustice of the world. Each stanza begins with the same sign, and the initial signs together form an acrostic that names the author, Saggil-kinam-ubbib, an incantation priest, as a worshipper of god and king. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/2/1/SB/-) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 258 of the 288 lines of the eBL edition (90%), from 10 tablets in the British Museum: K.8463 (Nineveh), BM.35405, K.9290 (Nineveh), BM.36704, BM.40098, K.17235 (Nineveh), K.1743 (Nineveh), BM.47745, BM.94273, K.3452 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 30 of the 288 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 89 (no manuscript preserves it); 109-110, 111-119 (no manuscript preserves it); 157 (no manuscript preserves it); 158-171 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.5932); 172 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.5932; quotation in another text: K.4267); 173-174 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.5932); 192 (no photograph in eBL: VAT.10567 (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin); commentary: BM.66882); 290-293 (no photograph in eBL: BM.34773, BM.34633); 294-297 (no photograph in eBL: BM.34773, BM.34633; commentary: BM.66882). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; * collated sign; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; < > sign omitted by the scribe, supplied by the editor; << >> sign written in error by the scribe; / alternative readings; : divider sign written on the tablet; @v and similar: variant or modified form of a sign; | division between the parts of a line written in separate columns on the tablet.

translation.text:
1[O my] sagacious [brother], come, let me tell you,
2The distress [I have seen, time and again], I would recount to you.
3Such deep misery [as has befallen me, may it weigh heavy] on your feelings,
4[In …] most distressful, I will always sing your praises:
5Where be the man of insight so able to advise?
6Whence the man of knowledge comparable to you?
7Where else to such a counsellor my woe could I relate?
8I was at a loss when heartache came upon me,
9I was the youngest child when fate carried off him who begot me,
10She who brought me into the world departed to the land of no return,
11My father and mother left me with no one to care for me!
12Considerate friend, what you tell is a sorrowful tale,
13My dear friend, you have let your creativity harbor ill.
14You make your estimable discretion feeble-minded,
15You alter your bright expression to a scowl.
16Our fathers are given up that they go death’s way,
17They will cross the river Hubur, as is commanded from of old.

18When you survey teeming humankind all around,
19If the poor man’s son is thriving, someone helped him prosper,
20Who did favors for the sleek and wealthy?
21He who looks to his god has a protector,
22The diffident man who reveres his goddess will garner wealth.
23My friend, your heart is a wellspring of depth unplumbed,
24The upsurging swell of the ocean that brooks no diminishment.
25To you, then, let me pose my questions, learn my drift,
26Hearken to me but for a moment, hear my declaration.
27Want and craving make up the covering of my body,
28I have outlived my success, (my) prime is past,
29(My) energies are gone feeble, (my) prospering is over,
30Moaning and woe have clouded [my] features.
31The sustenance from my tilth nowhere near suffices [me],
32Of the fruit of the vine, what sustains humankind, I am far from having enough.
33Can happy times be a certainty for me? I wish I knew how that might come about!
34My well-thought-out speech is the peak of good advice,
35Your wonted wisdom you transmute into ranting,
36You bring forward scatter-brained, irrational […],
37You render your choicest reasoning like a mountebank.
38As to your everlasting, unremitting desire is […]
39The angry god […] at the prayer of […].
40The estranged goddess returns upon supp[lication].
41If the … […] one gone astray […] forbearance,
42Seek constantly after the […] of doing what’s right.
43[The harshest …] will surely show kindness,
44He will lay wide [the way], he will surely grant [you] clemency.
45[I] have bowed [down before you], my [companion], I have absorbed [your] wisdom,
46[I have taken to heart the] honeyed discourse of [your] lips.
47Come, let me tell you what I understand:

48The onager, the wild ass, that had its fill of lush wild grasses,
49Did it have a care for the weighty wisdom of the gods?
50The savage lion that fed himself from the choicest meat,
51Did it bring its flour offerings to appease a goddess’s wrath?
52As to the rich magnate whose prosperity keeps increasing,
53Did he weigh out precious gold to the mother goddess?
54Have I withheld my offerings when I sacrificed to the god?
55When blessing the regular sacrifice to my goddess, have I ever been at fault?
56O date palm, wealth-giving tree, my treasured brother,
57Perfect in all wisdom, O gem [of wisdom]!
58If you are indeed fixed as the earth, the reasoning [of the gods] is far beyond (you).
59Consider on the […] that magnificent wild ass of the plain,
60An arrow will turn upon that one who trod every lea.
61Come, contemplate that lion you were thinking of, livestock’s bane,
62For the atrocities the lion committed, a pit yawns for him.
63The well-heeled rich man who hoarded up possessions,
64A sovereign will put him to the flames before his time.

65Would you wish to go the way these have gone?
66Seek after virtue’s reward from (your) god all your days.
67Your reasoning is a cool breeze, a breath of fresh air for humankind,
68Most particular friend, your advice is excellent.
69Let me put but one matter before you:
70Those who seek not after a god can go the road of favor,
71Those who pray to a goddess have grown poor and destitute.
72Indeed, in my youth I heeded the will of (my) god,
73With prayer and supplication I besought (my) goddess.
74I bore a yoke of profitless servitude:
75(My) god decreed (for me) penury instead of wealth.
76A cripple rises above me, a fool is ahead of me,
77A vile lackey is in the ascendant, I am demoted.
78Truly, O knowledgeable one, your ponderings are devoid of common sense,
79You have cast off truth, you have spurned divine design.
80In your emotional state you have felt an urge to disregard observances due (your) god,

translation.text:
235As for the vile lackey whose good fortune you craved,
236The verdure of the harvest, the pasture, will soon disappear.
237The godless reprobate who is grasping of possessions,
238The weapon of his deathblow is coming up behind him.
239Unless you heed the will of (your) god, what will be your gain?
240He who bears a god’s yoke will never want for food, though it may be meager.
241Seek after the favorable breeze of the gods,
242What you lost over a year you will recoup in a moment.
243I have looked around in society, indications are the contrary:
244God does not block the progress of a demon.
245A father hauls a boat up a channel,
246While his firstborn sprawls in bed.
247The eldest son sprints ahead like a lion,
248The younger brother is content to drive a donkey.
249The heir strolls the streets like an idler,
250The younger son makes provision for the destitute.
251What has it profited me that I knelt before a deity?
252It is I who must (now) bow before my inferior!

253The riffraff despise me, as do the rich and proud.
254Adept scholar, master of discernment,
255You blaspheme in the anguish of your thoughts.
256Divine purpose is as far beyond (you) as innermost heaven,
257It is too difficult to be conversant with, people cannot understand it.
258Among all living creatures, the handiwork of the birth-goddess,
259Why should offspring be completely without a say?
260The cow’s first calf is inferior,
261Her subsequent offspring is twice as big.
262The first child is born a weakling,
263The second is known as a capable warrior.
264Even if one (tries to) apprehend divine wisdom, people cannot understand it.
265Pay attention, my friend, learn my (next) parry,
266Consider the well-chosen diction of my speech.
267They extol the words of an important man who is accomplished in murder,
268They denigrate the powerless who has committed no crime.
269They esteem truthful the wicked to whom truth is abhorrent,

270They drive away the truthful man who heeds the will of god.
271They fill the oppressor’s strongroom with treasure,
272The larder of the helpless they empty of [his] provisions.
273They shore up the tyrant whose all is crime,
274They ruin the weak, they oppress the powerless.
275And as for me, without means, a magnate harasses me.
276Enlil, king of the gods, who created teeming humankind,
277Majestic Ea, who pinched off their clay,
278The queen who fashioned them, mistress Mami,
279Gave perverse words to the human race,
280They endowed them in perpetuity with lies and falsehood.
281Solemnly they speak well of a rich man,
282“He’s the king,” they say, “riches attend him.”
283They malign a poor man as a thief,
284They lavish malice upon him, they conspire to kill him.
285Like a criminal, they make him suffer every evil because he has no vault.
286They make him go numb with fear, they snuff him out like an ember.
287You are sympathetic, my friend, be considerate of (my) misfortune.
288Help me, see (my) distress, you should be cognizant of it.
289I am a suppliant, versatile servant,
